html:
The Adena culture was a way of life in the middle Ohio River valley, in today's Ohio, Kentucky and West Virginia, from about 500 BCE to about 100 CE. It is named after Adena, an estate near Chillicothe, Ohio, where a large mound was dug up in 1901. The map shows its area in 1492, long after it had ended; see also Adena culture.

The Adena people lived in small villages, hunted and gathered, and grew squash, sunflower and other native seed plants. They are known for their earth burial mounds, some very large, such as the Grave Creek Mound in West Virginia. Important people were buried with copper bracelets, carved stone pipes and mica from far away, a sign of long trade routes.

The Hopewell culture grew out of Adena and built on the same tradition of mounds and trade. Centuries later the Mississippian towns built their own, larger mounds in the same river system.
